input: This pricing case examines a SaaS tier and asks whether the current price covers the costs of providing the tier. The analysis follows the standard break-even approach, which separates the costs that vary with the number of units sold from the costs that are incurred regardless of volume. The price is $387 per unit, and the variable cost is $209 per unit, which means that each unit sold contributes $178 towards the fixed costs. The fixed costs amount to $304k per year. Dividing the fixed costs by the contribution per unit gives a break-even volume of 1708 units per year. Encouragingly, the current volume, at 3081 units per year, is comfortably above this level, so the tier is covering its fixed costs at the present price, with a considerable cushion before the break-even point would be reached. It should be noted that the volume figures used here are last year's actuals, and they therefore describe the position as it was rather than as it necessarily will be. It is also important to bear in mind that the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, so it cannot be assumed that the same volume would be achieved at a different price, and the break-even calculation would need to be revisited if the price were to change.
target: The SaaS tier covers its fixed costs at the current price and volume. The price is $387 per unit and the variable cost is $209 per unit, so each unit contributes $178 to fixed costs of $304k per year. Fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit give a break-even volume of 1708 units per year. Current volume is 3081 units per year (last year's actuals), above break-even by a wide margin. The finding rests on last year's volumes at last year's price. Break-even is the volume at which the contribution from the units sold exactly meets the fixed costs for the year. Below that volume the tier returns a loss; above it, each further unit sold adds its contribution to the surplus. The present position is therefore a statement about volume at the stated price, and the width of the margin above break-even is what protects the tier against a fall in volume. A fall in volume at the stated price erodes the surplus unit by unit at the contribution rate. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, and the break-even figure is not valid at a different price: at a lower price the contribution per unit falls and the break-even volume rises, by an amount the case does not quantify. The case likewise does not estimate the volume at the current price beyond last year's actual, so the margin is a record of last year, not a forecast.
